title: Flattening and combining
summary: SelectMany for nested data, Zip to walk two sequences side by side, Concat to append, Chunk to cut into pages.

steps.title: SelectMany is a nested loop
body: `Select` gives **one** output per input. `SelectMany` lets each input give **any number** of outputs (zero, one, many) and joins them into one flat sequence.
That is exactly a loop inside a loop:
Watch `"cde"` turn into three separate items, each continuing down the pipe on its own.

steps.prompt: HR has nobody in it. What does this print?
steps.explain: `Select` gives one array per department: 3. `SelectMany` flattens them: 2 + 0 + 3 = 5. An empty inner list adds nothing, so HR **disappears** from the flattened result. Keep that in mind when you need every department to show up (lesson 3 covers that).

steps.title: Keeping the parent: the result selector
body: After flattening, the inner item has forgotten which outer item it came from. The second lambda, the **result selector**, gets both:
In query syntax, a second `from` does the same, and reads like the nested loop it is:
var lines = from o in orders
There is also an overload whose lambda gets the outer item's **index**: `orders.SelectMany((o, i) => o.Items.Select(item => $"#{i} {item}"))`.

steps.prompt: Complete the query so it gives one `"Id: item"` line for every item in every order.
code: var lines = from o in orders
steps.explain: A second `from` is a `SelectMany`. The query still has to end with `select`.

steps.title: Zip and Concat
body: **`Zip`** walks two sequences **side by side**, pairing item 1 with item 1, item 2 with item 2, and so on. It stops when the **shorter** one runs out.
**`Concat`** puts one sequence after another: `names.Concat(new[] { "Di" })` is Ana, Bo, Cy, Di. Unlike `Union` (lesson 5) it keeps duplicates.
Zip replaces the "loop with an index into two arrays" pattern: `for (int i = 0; i < Math.Min(a.Length, b.Length); i++) ... a[i] ... b[i]`.

steps.explain: `Zip` stops at the shorter sequence, so `Cy` is dropped without any error. `Concat` keeps duplicates: 3 + 3 = 6. The last pair is `(Bo, 75)`, not `Cy`.

steps.title: Chunk: cut into pages
body: **`Chunk(n)`** groups consecutive items into arrays of `n`. The last array holds whatever is left.
Use it for paging, sending records to an API in batches of 100, or laying items out in rows. It replaces a loop that keeps a counter and starts a new list every `n` items.
`Select` has an overload that also gives you the **index**, handy for page numbers: `.Chunk(3).Select((page, i) => $"Page {i + 1}: ...")`.

steps.prompt: `a` has 3 items, `b` has 5, `lists` holds lists of sizes 2, 0 and 3. Match each call to what it gives.

steps.title: Nested loop to SelectMany

require.message: Flattens with SelectMany (or a second from)

hints: The inner loop needs the order's `Id`, so use the result selector: `SelectMany(o => o.Lines, (o, line) => ...)`.
Carry both in an anonymous object: `(o, line) => new { o.Id, line }`, then `Where` and `Select`.
Or in query syntax: `from o in orders from line in o.Lines where line.Qty > 0 select ...`.

steps.title: Invoice pages
prompt: `static List<string> Invoice(string[] items, decimal[] prices, int[] qtys)`: item `i` costs `prices[i]` and was bought `qtys[i]` times. One line per item as `"Pen 3 x 1.50 = 4.50"` (money with two decimals: `{x:0.00}`), then a final line `"TOTAL 9.50"`. If the arrays differ in length, ignore the extras (that is what `Zip` does).
`static List<string> Pages(List<string> lines, int perPage)`: cut the lines into pages and give one string per page: `"Page 1: a | b"`, `"Page 2: c"`.
starter: static List<string> Invoice(string[] items, decimal[] prices, int[] qtys)
static List<string> Pages(List<string> lines, int perPage)
solution: static List<string> Invoice(string[] items, decimal[] prices, int[] qtys)
.Select(t => new { Item = t.First, Price = t.Second, Qty = t.Third, Total = t.Second * t.Third })
static List<string> Pages(List<string> lines, int perPage)
template: Dojo.Eq("an invoice with a total", new List<string> { "Pen 3 x 1.50 = 4.50", "Pad 2 x 2.50 = 5.00", "TOTAL 9.50" },
Dojo.Eq("extra items without a price are ignored", new List<string> { "Ink 1 x 4.00 = 4.00", "TOTAL 4.00" },
Dojo.Eq("an empty invoice is only a total", new List<string> { "TOTAL 0.00" }, Invoice(new string[0], new decimal[0], new int[0]));
Dojo.Eq("Pages of 2", new List<string> { "Page 1: a | b", "Page 2: c | d", "Page 3: e" }, Pages(new List<string> { "a", "b", "c", "d", "e" }, 2));
Dojo.Eq("one big page", new List<string> { "Page 1: a | b" }, Pages(new List<string> { "a", "b" }, 10));
hints: Build the rows once with `ToList()`, so you can both print them and `Sum` them. Add the total line with `Concat(new[] { ... })`.

steps.title: Sidekick: the timesheet
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk timesheet` prints every time entry of the last week, one line each, ready for your manager. Write it with **SelectMany** and no loops.
`static List<string> TimesheetLines(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks, IEnumerable<TimeEntry> entries, DateOnly from, DateOnly to)`
- for each task, its entries whose `Day` is between `from` and `to` (both included). Use the `SelectMany` overload with a result selector so you keep the task next to each entry
- entries of tasks that are not in `tasks` are left out
- each line: date with weekday, start-end, the minutes with your `Sk.FormatMinutes` right-aligned in 7 characters, then the task code from `Ids.Format` and the title:
Formats: `{start:yyyy-MM-dd ddd}`, `{start:HH:mm}`, `{text,7}`. Two spaces between the parts.

Given in the tests, from your earlier Sidekick pieces: `TaskItem` (Id, Title, EstimateMinutes, LoggedMinutes, Done, IsRunning, Tag, Project, Due), `TimeEntry(int TaskId, DateTime Start, DateTime End)` with `Minutes` and `Day`, `Ids.Format` and `Sk.FormatMinutes`.
starter: static List<string> TimesheetLines(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks, IEnumerable<TimeEntry> entries, DateOnly from, DateOnly to) =>
solution: static List<string> TimesheetLines(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks, IEnumerable<TimeEntry> entries, DateOnly from, DateOnly to) => tasks
.SelectMany(t => entries.Where(e => e.TaskId == t.Id && e.Day >= from && e.Day <= to), (t, e) => (Task: t, Entry: e))
template: var dojoTasks = new List<TaskItem> { new(1, "Fix login redirect"), new(2, "Write parser tests"), new(3, "Plan the demo") };
DateTime DojoAt(int day, int h, int m) => new DateTime(2026, 11, day, h, m, 0);
var dojoWeek = TimesheetLines(dojoTasks, dojoEntries, new DateOnly(2026, 11, 23), new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25));
Dojo.Eq("one line per entry in the range", 4, dojoWeek.Count);

Dojo.Eq("from and to are both included", 2, TimesheetLines(dojoTasks, dojoEntries, new DateOnly(2026, 11, 23), new DateOnly(2026, 11, 23)).Count + TimesheetLines(dojoTasks, dojoEntries, new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25), new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25)).Count);
Dojo.Eq("an entry for a task that is not in the list is left out", false, dojoWeek.Any(l => l.Contains("SK-009")));
Dojo.Eq("no tasks, no lines", 0, TimesheetLines(new List<TaskItem>(), dojoEntries, new DateOnly(2026, 11, 1), new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30)).Count);
Dojo.Eq("an empty range", 0, TimesheetLines(dojoTasks, dojoEntries, new DateOnly(2026, 11, 26), new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30)).Count);

hints: `tasks.SelectMany(t => entries.Where(e => e.TaskId == t.Id && e.Day >= from && e.Day <= to), (t, e) => (Task: t, Entry: e))` keeps both.
steps.explain: The result selector of `SelectMany` is the LINQ version of a nested loop that can see both loop variables. Driving it from `tasks` is also an inner join for free: an entry whose task is gone never comes out.
